Let me analyze this specification carefully.

This is about Hyperledger Fabric channel configuration library. The user stories describe:

U1: Add orderer endpoint to an orderer org's config group - library function + example test
U2: Remove orderer endpoint from an orderer org's config group - library function + example test
U3: Retrieve existing policies for an organization (application/orderer/consortium org) + example test update
U4: Retrieve existing orderer, application, and channel capabilities from config transaction, returns config.Capabilities
U5: Add and remove application, orderer, and channel capabilities (consider toggles vs setting unsupported) + example test update
U6: Retrieve existing application configuration, returns config.Application
U7: Update application group's ACLs by adding or removing ACLs + example test update
U8: Split example usages into smaller, varied examples: orderer configuration, application values, organization management, MSP modifications, capabilities

This resembles the actual Fabric "config" library (github.com/hyperledger/fabric-config) work. The developer should:

1. Set up/understand existing codebase, design API
2. Implement U1: AddOrdererEndpoint
3. Implement U2: RemoveOrdererEndpoint
4. Implement U3: GetPolicies (for org - application/orderer/consortium)
5. Implement U4: GetCapabilities (orderer, application, channel)
6. Implement U5: Add/Remove capabilities for application, orderer, channel
7. Implement U6: GetApplicationConfiguration
8. Implement U7: Add/Remove ACLs
9. Implement U8: Refactor example tests into smaller examples
10. Unit tests for each
11. Integration/testing, documentation, code review, etc.

Technical and design decisions:
- Language: Go, consistent with Hyperledger Fabric codebase
- Leverage existing configtx library structures (cb.Config, ConfigGroup, etc.) and protolator for JSON marshaling
- API surface: exported functions operating on cb.Config, returning modified config; retrieval functions return config structs
- For U5: allow setting arbitrary capabilities rather than toggle functions, with validation against known capabilities optional — decide to support generic Add/Remove capability functions with string keys, per acceptance allowing further updates
- Define config.Application and config.Capabilities structs (new types) for retrieval functions
- Example tests in Go ExampleXxx style using a base config transaction fixture
- Unit tests with table-driven tests, use existing test fixtures/sample config blocks
- Modification functions preserve untouched parts of config so ConfigUpdate can be computed with existing tooling (configtx.ComputeUpdate)

Assumptions:
- Existing repo with config transaction update/computation utilities already exists (this is an increment on an existing library)
- Developer is proficient in Go and familiar with Fabric config structure; no ramp-up beyond initial analysis
- Effort includes unit tests and example tests; excludes setting up CI infrastructure, release packaging, and deployment
- No changes to Fabric core/peer binaries required; pure client library
- Test fixtures (sample channel config blocks) are available or can be generated from existing test utilities
- Code review is performed by a peer but rework effort included; review meeting time excluded
- Single developer, estimates in work-hours not elapsed time

technical_and_design_decisions: Implement in Go, consistent with the Hyperledger Fabric codebase, extending the existing channel configuration (configtx-style) library rather than creating a new module.

All modification functions will operate on a standard protobuf Config/ConfigGroup tree (cb.Config), navigating ChannelGroup -> orderer/application org groups -> Values, and will preserve all untouched fields so a ConfigUpdate can be computed afterward with the existing ComputeUpdate tooling.
For U1/U2, implement AddOrdererEndpoint and RemoveOrdererEndpoint functions that mutate the Endpoints value inside a named orderer org's config group.

For U3, implement a single GetPolicies-style retrieval that resolves the org group path differently for application, orderer, and consortium orgs, returning the policy map without manual parsing by the caller.
For U4, introduce a config.Capabilities wrapper type aggregating channel, orderer, and application capabilities retrieved from the respective Capability values.

For U5, implement generic Add/Remove capability functions keyed by capability string for each of channel, orderer, and application scopes (rather than hard-coded toggle functions), since generic setters also satisfy the toggle use case and support future capabilities; known-capability constants will be provided for convenience.
For U6, define a config.Application struct (organizations, capabilities, ACLs, policies) populated from the application group of the config transaction.
For U7, implement AddACL and RemoveACL functions mutating the ACLs value of the application group, re-serializing via protolator-compatible marshaling.

Use table-driven unit tests with existing sample channel config block fixtures; example tests written as Go Example functions for U8's split scenarios (orderer config, application values, org management, MSP, capabilities).
assumptions: An existing library codebase is in place with Config/ConfigUpdate computation utilities and test fixtures; this increment adds functions to it (no greenfield setup).
The developer is proficient in Go and already familiar with Fabric channel config protobuf structures; only modest design/analysis ramp-up is needed.
Estimates include implementation, unit tests, and example test updates; they exclude CI pipeline setup, release packaging, and deployment.
No changes to Fabric core (peer/orderer binaries) are required; this is a client-side configuration library increment.
Sample channel config blocks covering orderer orgs, application orgs, consortiums, capabilities, ACLs, and MSP are available from existing test utilities.
Code review feedback rework is included; the reviewer's own time is excluded since the developer performs all work alone.
Where the spec is ambiguous (U5 toggle vs. generic setters), the generic approach above is assumed and no further clarification is needed.

activities.activity_description: Analyze U1-U8, inspect the existing codebase, define function signatures and new types (config.Capabilities, config.Application), and decide the generic capability setter approach for U5.
Implement function to add an orderer endpoint to an orderer org's config group, with unit tests and a demonstration snippet for the example test.
Implement function to remove an orderer endpoint from an orderer org's config group, with unit tests and a demonstration snippet (reuses U1 patterns).
Implement policy retrieval for a specific org covering application, orderer, and consortium org group paths; unit tests and example test update.
Implement retrieval of channel, orderer, and application capabilities from a config transaction returning a config.Capabilities value, with unit tests.
Implement add and remove capability functions for application, orderer, and channel scopes (six functions) plus known-capability constants; unit tests and example test update.
Implement retrieval of the full application group configuration returning a config.Application (orgs, ACLs, policies, capabilities), with unit tests.
Implement functions to add and remove ACL entries in the application group's ACLs value; unit tests and example test update.

Split the single end-to-end example into focused examples: orderer configuration (with orderer policies), application values (with application policies), organization management (orgs, anchor peers, orderer endpoints), MSP modifications, and capabilities; integrate U1-U3/U5/U7 demonstrations.
Write godoc comments for all new exported functions and types, and update README/package documentation with the new capabilities.
Run full test suites, verify ConfigUpdate computation works end-to-end on modified configs (acceptance criteria), self-review code, and apply rework/fixes.
